comments.body: I just realized I accidentally changed the version. I hope it's okay.
This app is Win32-based, not UWP. Is it possible to use StartupTask with it?

The project name is `RunCat365` (without a space) because spaces are not allowed, but the correct display name for the app is `RunCat 365` (with a space). Please do not change this. In fact, please avoid including changes that are unrelated to the main purpose of the pull request.
Could you please explain the effect of these changes?
If it is packaged (which is done for the Microsoft Store) yes. If it is not packaged, you can use the method you used before. I made the code so that I could handle both cases.
As I mentioned I did to avoid conflicts, but if you want we can leave it as it was.

Is it necessary to separate the logic for the Store version and the non-Store version? Will a common logic not work for both? Also, since I have no plans to distribute this outside of the Store, I believe the logic for the non-Store version is unnecessary.
`MessageBox.Show` is a UI-related operation, right? Please separate the UI logic from the business logic. At the very least, I'd prefer not to have UI-related code directly in `Program.cs`.
It is so that it ignores elements that are not mandatory.
If someone downloads the source from here, GitHub, they won't be able to run the app unless they package it. Still, I leave it to your consideration.
Understood
You are right. It was like this because of a previous logic that I ended up discarding. And I forgot to correct that.
After investigating, I've come to understand that this is added automatically by Visual Studio and seems to be unavoidable.

So, does this prevent the app from running, or just disable the 'Launch at startup' feature? If the app can't run, the branching is probably needed. 
However, for local builds, we should just hide the 'Launch at startup' menu item for non-packaged versions to avoid confusing users (or developers) with a disabled option.

Still, if you want to support both cases, it would be better to implement them in separate child functions and have `GetStartupAsync` and `SetStartupAsync` call those functions accordingly. My impression is that the current implementation might add to our maintenance overhead. I'd be open to it, though, if you could refactor it into a cleaner and more readable design.

> So, does this prevent the app from running, or just disable the 'Launch at startup' feature?

If your app isn't packaged, it basically uses the feature you had before you removed it.

---

> However, for local builds, we should just hide the 'Launch at startup' menu item for non-packaged versions to avoid confusing users (or developers) with a disabled option.

It's not that it's disabled, it just works differently when it's packaged than when it's not.

---

> Still, if you want to support both cases, it would be better to implement them in separate child functions and have `GetStartupAsync` and `SetStartupAsync` call those functions accordingly.

I understand, you're right. 

---

> I'd be open to it, though, if you could refactor it into a cleaner and more readable design.

I will work on it. Thank you.
Since this is a 'Launch at startup' feature, names like `getLaunchAtStartup` or `toggleLaunchAtStartup` would be more appropriate.
This applies to the whole thing as well.

Wouldn't it be better to initialize and hold the Manager instance in `Program.cs`? 
Do you have a specific reason for wanting it to be a static function?

Instead of calling `MessageBox.Show()` here, it would be better to throw an error and handle it in the `ContextMenuManager` that uses `SetStartup`. 
Since `ContextMenuManager` deals with UI-related operations, it makes more sense there.
